Helping Children and Adolescents Feel Safe, Supported and Understood After Trauma

When a child or teenager experiences something frightening, overwhelming or deeply upsetting, their response may not always be easy to understand.

Some children talk about what happened. Others become quieter, more irritable, clingy or withdrawn. Some may appear to be coping well at first and show changes later.

There is no single "right" response to trauma.

What matters is that children and adolescents have safe, supportive adults around them and, when needed, access to appropriate professional support. Children's Health Queensland recommends reassurance, calm and honest communication, age-appropriate information, predictable routines and ongoing check-ins after a traumatic event.

At MBP, we can help families understand what may be happening and guide you towards an appropriate practitioner for your child or teenager.

What Is Childhood Trauma?

Trauma can occur when a child or adolescent experiences, witnesses or is affected by an event or situation that feels frightening, overwhelming or threatening to their sense of safety.

Potentially traumatic experiences can include:

  • Serious accidents or injuries
  • Unexpected death or loss of someone important
  • Witnessing violence or domestic violence
  • Abuse, neglect or family violence
  • Medical experiences or serious illness
  • Natural disasters or other major emergencies
  • Bullying or other frightening experiences
  • Exposure to conflict or other highly distressing events
  • Other experiences that significantly affect a child's sense of safety or wellbeing

Not every child who experiences a difficult event will develop ongoing trauma-related difficulties. Children respond differently depending on their age, development, previous experiences, temperament, relationships and the support available to them.

Recent Australian research highlights how common potentially traumatic experiences during childhood can be. A University of Sydney-led study using nationally representative Australian data found that 42% of adults had experienced at least one potentially traumatic event before the age of 18. The researchers found an association between childhood trauma and a substantially higher likelihood of mental health or substance-use disorders later in life.

This reinforces the importance of early, supportive and trauma-informed care without assuming that every child who experiences trauma will develop a mental health condition.

Trauma Can Look Different in Every Child

Children do not always have the words to explain what they are experiencing.

Instead, distress may show up through changes in behaviour, emotions, sleep, relationships, school participation or physical wellbeing.

A child or teenager may experience:

  • Trouble falling asleep or changes in sleep
  • Nightmares
  • Increased clinginess or separation anxiety
  • Wanting more reassurance than usual
  • Irritability, anger or emotional outbursts
  • Becoming unusually quiet or withdrawn
  • Losing interest in activities they normally enjoy
  • Difficulty concentrating
  • Increased worry or fear
  • Changes in behaviour at home or school
  • Physical complaints such as headaches or stomach aches
  • Younger children returning to behaviours they had previously grown out of

Children's Health Queensland notes that these reactions can vary considerably between children and may be expressed through behaviour rather than words. Many reactions ease with time, safety and supportive relationships.

When a Child Has Been Through Something Frightening

A child's first need after a traumatic event is often to feel safe again.

Parents and carers do not need to have the perfect explanation or know exactly what to say. Helpful responses can include:

Reassure safety

A calm, supportive adult can help a child feel more secure.

Listen before explaining

Find out what your child understands about what happened. Children may have heard information from friends, school, television or social media that is incomplete or inaccurate.

Be honest and age-appropriate

Children benefit from information they can understand without being overwhelmed by unnecessary detail.

Acknowledge their feelings

Fear, sadness, anger, confusion or uncertainty can all occur after a frightening experience. Children may communicate these feelings through their behaviour rather than directly talking about them.

Maintain familiar routines

Regular routines can provide predictability and a sense of stability while a child is adjusting.

Keep checking in

One conversation may not be enough. A child may have questions or feelings that emerge later. These approaches are consistent with current Queensland children's health guidance following traumatic events.

You May Be Looking for Support Because...

You may be wondering whether your child's response to a traumatic experience is within the expected range, or whether additional support could help.

You might notice that your child:

  • Seems significantly different from how they were before
  • Continues to experience distress after the event
  • Is struggling with sleep or regular routines
  • Becomes increasingly anxious, angry or withdrawn
  • Finds school or everyday activities more difficult
  • Avoids situations connected with what happened
  • Has difficulty talking about or making sense of their experience
  • Is having difficulties with friendships or family relationships
  • Seems unable to settle even when they are in a safe environment
  • Is experiencing ongoing changes that are affecting daily life

The aim is not to label every reaction as trauma. Rather, professional support can help clarify what your child is experiencing and what type of support may be appropriate.

Trauma and Adolescence

Trauma can be particularly complicated during adolescence because young people are already navigating changes in identity, independence, friendships, family relationships and school or future expectations.

A teenager may not want to talk directly about what happened. They may instead communicate distress through changes in behaviour, withdrawal, irritability, difficulties at school or changes in relationships.

A trauma-informed approach recognises that behaviour can sometimes communicate distress rather than simply being viewed as "bad behaviour."

The University of Sydney research has also highlighted the importance of recognising trauma-related difficulties early and responding with supportive, trauma-informed care across the systems that children and young people interact with, including health and education.

When Professional Support May Help

Many children recover from difficult experiences with the support of family, trusted adults and their existing routines.

However, additional support may be helpful when distress:

  • Continues for weeks after the event
  • Becomes more intense rather than settling
  • Interferes with school, sleep, relationships or everyday activities
  • Is difficult for the family to manage
  • Causes ongoing anxiety, withdrawal or emotional distress
  • Makes it difficult for the child to return to activities they previously enjoyed

Children's Health Queensland recommends considering additional support when signs of distress continue after the event or begin interfering with daily activities.

You can begin by speaking with your GP, school support team or an appropriately qualified child or adolescent mental health professional.

How Trauma Therapy Can Help

Trauma therapy is not about forcing a child to repeatedly talk about what happened. A trauma-informed practitioner considers the child's age, developmental stage, individual circumstances and readiness.

Depending on the child's needs, therapy may focus on:

Feeling safe again

Helping the child understand and strengthen their sense of safety and stability.

Understanding their reactions

Helping children and teenagers make sense of changes in emotions, thoughts, behaviour and physical responses.

Developing coping skills

Building practical strategies for managing anxiety, strong emotions, worries and reminders of difficult experiences.

Processing difficult experiences

When appropriate, therapy can provide a safe and developmentally appropriate way to work through aspects of the experience.

Rebuilding confidence

Supporting children to reconnect with school, friendships, activities and everyday life.

Strengthening communication

Helping children communicate their needs and helping parents understand what their child may be trying to express.

Supporting parents and carers

Parents can also benefit from guidance about how to respond, communicate and provide consistent support at home.

The specific approach will depend on the child, the nature of the experience and the practitioner's qualifications and clinical recommendations.

What Could Change With the Right Support?

The goal of trauma-informed support is not to erase what happened.

It may instead help a child or teenager:

  • Feel safer and more settled
  • Understand their reactions
  • Develop healthier coping strategies
  • Communicate difficult emotions
  • Manage reminders or worries
  • Rebuild confidence
  • Return to school and everyday activities
  • Strengthen relationships with parents, carers and peers
  • Feel more capable of handling future challenges

Recovery does not necessarily happen in a straight line. A child may have good days and difficult days while adjusting.

With appropriate support, children can develop a stronger understanding of their experiences and greater confidence in managing what comes next.

Trauma-Informed Support for Families

Parents often wonder:

"Did I handle it the right way?"

You do not need to have perfect words.

Children's Health Queensland emphasises that children benefit most from calm, honest and supportive adults who are willing to listen and stay alongside them as they process what has happened.

A trauma-informed approach also means looking beyond the behaviour itself and asking what the child may be communicating or needing.

Sometimes a child who is angry, withdrawn, distracted or struggling at school is communicating distress rather than simply choosing to behave poorly.

Understanding the underlying need can change how adults respond.

You Don't Need to Know Where to Start

Finding the right support after a traumatic experience can feel overwhelming, particularly when you are unsure whether your child's reactions are "serious enough" to need therapy. You don't have to figure it out alone.

MBP provides an administrative starting point for families looking for psychological and mental health support. We can help you understand the next steps and identify an appropriate practitioner based on your child's age, needs, location and the type of support being sought. Not every practitioner offers trauma therapy, and the most appropriate approach will depend on your child's individual circumstances.
